strengths: The paper identifies a clean and conceptually appealing connection between multicalibration (a fairness notion) and the algorithms-with-predictions literature: it shows how to post-process an arbitrary black-box predictor so that a single fixed optimal decision rule (e.g., Edmonds' algorithm) applied to the calibrated output is competitive with the best rule in a class C applied to the original predictor.

The motivating example (two-armed setting where an unbiased estimator is arbitrarily bad under arg max) is illuminating and effectively motivates why unbiasedness alone is insufficient and why multicalibration-type guarantees are needed.

The core theorem (Theorem 1) and its proof are clearly presented; the argument decomposing the guarantee into two multicalibration conditions (one on the original C-induced partition of contexts, one on the calibrated predictor's own optimal matching) is a nice modular way to adapt the omnipredictor-style proof technique to a combinatorial optimization setting.

The framework generalizes beyond matching to other linear optimization problems with combinatorial constraints (matroids, learning with rejection), which strengthens the significance of the contribution and shows the approach is not narrowly tied to matching.

The sample complexity analysis (Theorem 2) is instance-adaptive: the number of iterations/samples needed scales with the mean-squared error r of the initial predictor relative to the Bayes-optimal predictor, which is a meaningful refinement over pure worst-case bounds and is argued to be realistic for well-trained industrial predictors.

The related work section is thorough and carefully situates the contribution relative to closely related recent work (including explicit discussion of the concurrent Kiyani et al. 2025 paper), which aids assessment of novelty.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments, simulations, or empirical illustration (not even on synthetic data) to demonstrate that the proposed multicalibration procedure yields practical improvements over naive or alternative baselines; for a claim in the title ('yields better matchings') this is a significant gap for assessing real-world applicability.

The sample complexity bounds are quite large in the relevant problem parameters (Õ(n^8/ε^4) or Õ(n^8/ε^2) under an optimistic MSE assumption), and the paper does not discuss whether these bounds are tight, nor does it provide any lower bound, making it hard to judge how much slack exists between the analysis and reality.

The paper explicitly notes that an alternative, simpler approach (directly estimating the expected performance of each rule in C and selecting the best) achieves better sample complexity (Õ(n^4/ε^2 log|C|) vs. Õ(n^8/ε^4 log|C|)); the claimed advantages of the proposed method (improved MSE, reusability of a single fixed algorithm) are stated qualitatively but not quantified or empirically compared, leaving the practical trade-off between the two approaches unclear.

The technical machinery is explicitly an adaptation of existing weighted multicalibration algorithms and analysis from Gopalan et al. (2022b) and Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018) to a vector-valued, non-simplex setting; while the specific application to combinatorial decision rules (matching, matroids) via the choice of weight classes W1, W2 is a reasonable and useful instantiation, the core proof techniques (potential-function convergence, CHECK oracle sample complexity) closely follow prior work, somewhat limiting technical originality.

The framework requires C to be finite and fixed a priori; there is no discussion of how to handle continuous or very large/infinite families of decision rules, nor of the computational (as opposed to sample) cost of running CHECK when |C| or the weight class W1 is large, which could be substantial in practice given W1 has one entry per (c, edge) pair.

There is limited discussion of limitations: e.g., no acknowledgment of how loose the worst-case bounds might be in realistic regimes, no discussion of practical computational bottlenecks of the boosting-style Algorithm 1, and no sensitivity analysis on how the results degrade for approximate or non-optimal solvers c* beyond a brief mention in the introduction.

strengths: Conceptually interesting connection between the fairness notion of multicalibration and the algorithms-with-predictions framework, in particular applied to a combinatorial optimization task (max-weight matching) rather than classification.

The core result (Theorem 1) is clean: a multicalibrated predictor's induced matching is competitive (up to additive error) with the best decision rule from a fixed class C applied to the original predictor. The proof is short and correct.

The framework is shown to generalize naturally to other linear-maximization-with-constraints settings (best action selection, learning with rejection, matroid-constrained maximization), illustrating some flexibility of the approach.

The sample complexity analysis (Theorem 2) is refined beyond worst case by relating the number of boosting iterations to the mean-squared error of the initial predictor relative to the Bayes-optimal one, which is a nice technical touch.
Related work is reasonably thorough and correctly situates the paper with respect to very recent/concurrent work (Kiyani et al., 2025).
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical, with no experiments, synthetic simulations, or any empirical demonstration that the proposed multicalibration-based pipeline actually yields practical benefits for matching or any of the extended settings. Given the paper's motivation is explicitly practical (industry predictors, imperfect black-box models), the complete absence of empirical validation is a serious gap that undermines the significance claims.

The paper openly acknowledges that a simpler alternative (directly estimate the expected performance of each rule in C and commit to the best one) achieves the same competitive guarantee with strictly fewer samples (O(n^4/ε^2 log|C|) vs O(n^8/ε^4 log|C|)). The claimed advantages of the proposed approach (improving the original predictor in MSE sense, reusability of a single downstream algorithm) are asserted only qualitatively and never quantified or empirically substantiated, leaving the core motivation for preferring the more complex and sample-hungry multicalibration route unclear.

The derived sample-complexity bounds are extremely large (polynomial of degree 8 in n, inverse-quartic in ε), which raises doubts about practical relevance for anything but very small graphs/ε, yet the paper argues for 'realistic' applicability based on an unverified assumption about predictor MSE scaling as O(ε^2).

Section 4 ('Other Models') only sketches extensions informally, without stating them as formal theorems or providing proofs; the reader must trust that 'the same analysis carries over' without seeing the details, which is not fully rigorous for a theory-focused paper.

The technical machinery is a fairly direct adaptation of existing weighted multicalibration techniques (Gopalan et al., 2022b; Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018) to a vector-valued/regression setting and a specific choice of weight class tailored to matching decisions; the novelty is primarily in the application/weight-class construction rather than in new algorithmic or statistical techniques.

The comparison with the concurrent and closely related work of Kiyani et al. (2025) is brief; given the apparent overlap in goals (post-processing calibrated/partially-calibrated predictors so that argmax decisions are near-optimal), a more detailed technical comparison (e.g., what is lost/gained by the minimax formulation there vs. the competitive-ratio formulation here) would strengthen the positioning of the contribution.

The practical relevance of the chosen weight class W (which requires knowledge of C and of the structure of the matching problem to construct, and is used only in the pre-processing/calibration phase) is not stressed enough: constructing and checking membership for W1, especially when C is large or continuous, could be computationally nontrivial, yet this is not discussed.

strengths: The paper makes a conceptually interesting connection between multicalibration (a fairness notion) and algorithms-with-predictions settings for combinatorial optimization, extending multicalibration's machinery (originally for bias auditing) to 'protect' events of the form 'edge e is chosen by decision rule c'. This is a genuinely novel use of the tool.

Theorem 1's proof is clean and intuitive, cleverly chaining two multicalibration conditions (one on the original predictor's induced matchings via W1, one on the final predictor's matching via W2) to sandwich the performance gap.

The framework is shown to generalize naturally beyond matching to any linear optimization with matroid constraints (max-weight independent set) and to the best-action/learning-with-rejection settings, demonstrating some versatility of the approach.

The refined sample-complexity analysis (Theorem 2) ties iteration/sample counts to the mean-squared error of the initial predictor relative to Bayes-optimal, giving a more realistic picture than pure worst-case bounds and connecting theory to practically plausible regimes (small MSE from large-scale industrial training).
Good situating within the multicalibration literature, including an honest and specific comparison to concurrent work (Kiyani et al. 2025).
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with zero empirical validation, even a small simulated experiment to illustrate the practical gain of using multicalibration over the naive baseline (estimate each rule's performance and commit to the best) would substantially strengthen the claims; as presented, it is unclear whether the proposed pipeline offers tangible benefits in realistic regimes versus the simpler alternative.

The authors' own comparison shows the naive alternative (estimate-and-commit) requires asymptotically fewer samples (O~(n^4/epsilon^2) vs O~(n^8/epsilon^4)); the stated advantages (points (i) and (ii) in the Introduction) are somewhat qualitative/soft and not rigorously shown to outweigh this sample-complexity gap in any formalized sense (e.g., no lower bound showing the naive approach cannot achieve property (i) or (ii), or a quantified trade-off).

The sample complexity bounds, even under the 'realistic' MSE assumption, remain very high-degree polynomials in n (O~(n^8/epsilon^2)), raising questions about practical relevance for the graph sizes and precision regimes of interest; the paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of when these bounds are actually informative/non-vacuous.

The restriction to a finite class C (with sample complexity scaling as log|C|) limits the scope of applicability; it's not discussed how this framework would extend or degrade for infinite/continuous families of decision rules, which seems like a natural practical case.

Algorithm 1 and Theorem 2 rely on oracle access to a CHECK procedure without much discussion of its computational feasibility or cost in the matching setting, where naively checking violations over W1 (indexed by all c in C) and auditing over matchings could be computationally demanding; this gap between statistical and computational complexity is not addressed.

The presentation, while generally clear, leaves some notational/formal gaps, e.g., the informal treatment of x as an implicit argument in Theorem 1's proof, and limited intuition given for why W1 and W2 specifically suffice (beyond the proof mechanics) could be elaborated for readability.
